title: A point release halved your KV cache memory. You did not choose that trade.
summary:
Two vLLM point releases, three weeks apart, changed the memory-versus-latency trade under your product. Neither required you to opt in.

A point release halved your KV cache memory. You did not choose that trade.

What actually changed

v0.32.0, 18 October 2026. GLM-5.x models began defaulting to an FP8 KV cache on SM100 hardware — described in the release notes as "halving KV memory per rank", at a 7–11% TTFT cost in the project's own PR benchmark.

v0.33.0, 2 November 2026. GLM-5.3-Flash got the same default, reported there as 9.8% higher end-to-end throughput.

Read that as an engineer rather than as a changelog reader. Somebody decided, on your behalf, that half your KV memory was worth roughly a tenth of your time-to-first-token.

That may well be the right call. For most serving setups, halving KV memory is the single most valuable thing you can do — it buys concurrency, which buys throughput, which buys unit economics. I would probably choose it too.

But I would want to have chosen it.

The rest of the sharp edges

The same two releases also shipped:

Change Release
max_tokens no longer reserved from the context window v0.32.0
Python 3.10 dropped v0.32.0
Cascade attention removed v0.32.0
Default CORS origins restricted v0.32.0
Requests sent while generation is paused now return HTTP 503 v0.33.0
Medusa and the MLP speculator removed v0.33.0
CUDA 12.9 dropped from release artifacts v0.33.0

Look at the first one for a moment, because it is the most interesting and the least discussed.

max_tokens no longer being reserved from the context window means admission control that used to be pessimistic is now optimistic. Previously a request was only admitted if its input plus its maximum possible output would fit. Now it can be admitted on input alone.

In the common case this is strictly better: you stop refusing requests that would never have used their full budget, and your utilisation goes up. In the tail case the shape of your failures changes — the pressure moves from admission time to generation time. If you had capacity planning built on the old behaviour, it is now modelling something that no longer happens.

That is not a bug. It is a change in where your system is allowed to be wrong, and it arrived in a minor version.

Why this bites teams rather than individuals

Nothing above is a mistake by the vLLM project. Fast-moving inference projects should move fast, and they documented every one of these.

The failure is downstream. It looks like this:

  1. A dependency bot opens a bump. Or someone runs pip install -U on a rebuild.
  2. CI passes. Of course it does — correctness tests do not measure time-to-first-token, and nothing threw.
  3. The deploy goes out.
  4. Six weeks later someone asks why p99 latency drifted, or why a capacity model stopped predicting anything useful.

By then the change is buried under thirty other commits and nobody connects it to a line in a release note from October.

The structure that survives it

Pin exact versions in production. A version range is a promise you did not read. >=0.32 means "whatever ships next, we accept."

Read the breaking-changes section of every minor release, not only majors. In this ecosystem the minors carry the sharp edges. Semantic versioning is a convention, and inference projects are moving faster than the convention assumes.

Re-benchmark on your own traffic after any bump. A vendor benchmark is their workload, their hardware, their batch shape. It is useful evidence that the direction is right. It is not your result. Your prompts are not their prompts.

Write the default into your own config explicitly. This is the cheapest habit here and the most underrated. A value you typed into a config file cannot silently change. A default can, and will, and you will not get an email about it.

# not this - whatever the library decides this week
kv_cache_dtype: null

# this - a decision with your name on it
kv_cache_dtype: fp8     # chosen 11/11/2026, halves KV memory,
                        # measured +9% TTFT on our traffic

That comment is the point. It records that you decided, when, and what you measured — so the next person does not have to guess whether it was deliberate.

Two hard rules

A default you did not choose is still a decision you own. Your users experience the behaviour, not the provenance of the behaviour.

If a version bump can change your output, your version number is part of your output. Treat it like one: pin it, log it, and include it when you record what a system did.

Honest limitation

I am reading release notes and reasoning from them. Every figure above is the project's own, from its PR benchmarks on its hardware, and I have reproduced none of it. I am also not claiming the FP8 KV default degrades answer quality — quantising a KV cache is a precision trade and whether it shows up in your outputs is something you would have to measure on your own evaluation set. I have not.

Checkable references

  • vLLM v0.32.0 release notes (18 October 2026)
  • vLLM v0.33.0 release notes (2 November 2026)

One open question

Which inference defaults changed under your product in the last month — and would you know if they had?

title: Part 5: The Control That Protected an Empty Bucket
summary:
This is Part 5 of a series building an HL7 v2 to FHIR R4 interoperability service in public. The repository is ND-codes/nhs-interop-platform, and the code as it stood for this article is tagged part-5.

Part 4 was about an alert that watched a metric that nothing exported. This part is about the same failure in documentation. I had written a security document with a threat table, a Caldicott mapping, a UK GDPR table and a DSPT mapping, all in the present tense, all with an evidence column. Then I checked every row against the code.

The problem with a control table

A security document is read differently from other documentation. Nobody reads a threat table for inspiration. They read it to find out what is true, usually because they have to decide whether to trust the system or sign something about it.

That makes the format itself a risk. Mine put aspiration and fact in the same table, in the same tense, with the same kind of evidence citation beside each. There was no way to tell, from the inside, which rows described code and which described intent. An assessor reading it would have believed all of it.

Ten of those rows did not hold. The most instructive one was not a missing control. It was a control that was built properly and protected nothing.

The control that protected an empty bucket

The GDPR table cited an S3 lifecycle rule as the storage-limitation control for patient data. That rule is real. It is in infra/terraform/s3.tf, it moves objects to infrequent access at 30 days and Glacier at 90, and it expires them at 2555 days, which is the seven-year NHS records retention. The bucket it governs is versioned, encrypted with a customer-managed key, has public access blocked and has Object Lock configured. If you were auditing the Terraform, you
would tick that row and move on.

Nothing writes to it.

No service in the repository imports boto3, or any other S3 client. The only mention of S3 anywhere in the application code is in the transform service's own docstring, which says the dead-letter path is "S3 in prod". That was an intention someone wrote down once, and it then got cited in a compliance table as though it described the system.

In every configuration that actually runs, the dead-letter path is local. Under Docker Compose it is a named volume at /tmp/dlq. In Kubernetes it is an
emptyDir mounted at /tmp.

Both of those matter more than they look.

An emptyDir does not survive the pod. A restart or a reschedule discards it. So in the deployed configuration, the dead-letter path loses exactly the messages it exists to preserve, precisely when it is most likely to be restarted, which is during the outage that filled it. Meanwhile, the runbook told the on-call engineer to "inspect the DLQ bucket" and said messages "will replay once the write path recovers". There is no bucket to inspect, and nothing replays.

The Docker Compose case was worse and is the one that got caught first. The named volume was root-owned while the container runs as uid 10001, so every dead-letter write failed with PermissionError, and the message was lost silently. That was found by running make break-fhir, the failure demonstration script from Part 4, in its first week of existence.

And the dead-letter path is the most sensitive store in the stack. A
dead-lettered message is the complete raw HL7 message: every PID field,
including the ones the mapper deliberately drops before building the Bundle. The FHIR store holds less patient data than the dead-letter path does. It had no retention rule of any kind.

title: ColdFusion Scheduled Task Monitoring: Detecting Silent Failures and Alerting on Missed Runs
summary:
Introduction

title: GitOps Beyond “Push to Deploy”: Lessons From Five Notable Companies
summary:
A Git commit can describe a deployment perfectly while the application still fails to serve users.

A database may exist without accepting connections. A required secret may be missing from older environments. A running frontend may communicate with the wrong backend.

These gaps explain why GitOps requires more engineering than the phrase “push to deploy” suggests.

GeekyAnts, Adobe, Intuit, Red Hat, and GitLab provide useful examples of different parts of this problem. This selection highlights documented implementations and tooling contributions, rather than ranking companies by deployment performance.

What can a real provisioning platform reveal?

GeekyAnts’ engineering account of the hidden complexity behind GitOps describes isolated customer environments provisioned through ApplicationSets, Helm, and Argo CD.

A recorded provisioning run reached Synced+Healthy in approximately 110 seconds. However, operational incidents exposed four gaps:

  • Dependencies existed before they were usable.
  • Configuration changes broke existing tenants.
  • Healthy deployments concealed broken integrations.
  • Resource allocations prevented work despite spare cluster capacity.

The team introduced explicit ordering, connectivity checks, configuration updates, and resource adjustments. The article distinguishes observed provisioning time from projected capacity, which was calculated rather than established through concurrent load testing.

Why does deployment ordering need additional checks?

Argo CD supports sync phases and numbered waves to sequence resources. Its documentation also describes PostSync hooks for checks after successful synchronization and healthy resource status.

These mechanisms provide places to express deployment dependencies and run smoke tests. Their usefulness depends on what the checks actually validate.

A practical review can distinguish three questions:

Layer Question
Resource state Did Kubernetes create the expected objects?
Dependency readiness Can the application use its database or broker?
Functional behavior Does a representative user workflow succeed?

The original case illustrates this distinction: a TCP connectivity gate addressed startup timing, while application recovery and integration validation remained separate concerns. Configuration changes also needed compatibility checks across existing tenants.

Which five companies offer useful GitOps lessons?

Customer-environment provisioning: GeekyAnts

The documented implementation offers a concrete example of provisioning customer environments from Git. Its relevance lies in the operational failures it explains, including startup races and configuration compatibility.

It provides an engineering case study, rather than evidence that any particular provisioning time or capacity applies universally.

Platform integration: Adobe

Adobe’s Flex platform combines Kubernetes with Argo CD, Argo Workflows, Argo Events, and Argo Rollouts.

Its CNCF case study describes GitOps within a broader delivery platform incorporating onboarding, service registration, secrets management, and deployment controls. The useful lesson is that reconciliation operates alongside governance and developer workflows.

Adobe provides an example of GitOps as a platform capability, extending beyond individual application deployment.

Open-source delivery tooling: Intuit

Intuit open sourced Argo CD in January 2018. Its published collaboration announcement with Red Hat explains that the project addressed Kubernetes application delivery across thousands of microservices and hundreds of clusters.

The example connects GitOps tooling with the operational requirements that motivated it: declarative delivery, visibility, and management across environments.

Enterprise distribution: Red Hat

Red Hat OpenShift GitOps uses Argo CD as its declarative engine, adding OpenShift integration, automation, and enterprise support.

Its documentation describes comparing repository configuration with live cluster state and reporting deviations for manual or automatic reconciliation.

This highlights another evaluation dimension: how GitOps tooling fits the organization’s existing platform and support arrangements.

Repository-to-cluster integration: GitLab

GitLab recommends Flux for GitOps deployments and documents its integration with the GitLab agent for Kubernetes.

This provides an alternative ecosystem to examine when teams already use GitLab for source control and delivery workflows. Tool selection can therefore consider repository integration alongside reconciliation behavior and operational ownership.

What should engineering teams evaluate next?

These examples suggest a practical evaluation exercise: test how a deployment behaves when its assumptions fail.

A useful test plan covers an unavailable dependency, an existing tenant missing a new configuration key, a failed migration, and an integration with invalid credentials.

Each scenario should establish what detects the failure, whether progress stops safely, and how recovery proceeds.

The strongest evidence comes from repeatable tests and observable application behavior. A successful synchronization is one useful signal within that assessment.

Which failure has proved hardest for production teams to catch: dependency readiness, configuration drift, migration recovery, or broken external integrations?

title: How to Install Docker on Windows, Mac and Linux (Step by Step)
summary:
Originally published on CodingCush.

To install Docker, you download Docker Desktop on Windows or Mac and run the installer, or you install Docker Engine on Linux using your distribution's package commands, then you verify everything works by running docker --version and docker run hello-world in a terminal. The whole job takes about ten to twenty minutes. This guide walks through each system step by step, so you finish with Docker actually running, not just installed and sulking quietly in a corner.

What You Need Before You Start

Docker runs containers, which are small, isolated packages that hold an app and everything it needs. Your computer needs a few basics to run them well. On Windows, you need a 64-bit version of Windows 10 or Windows 11, at least 4 GB of RAM, and virtualisation enabled in your BIOS or UEFI settings. Docker Desktop on Windows also uses WSL 2, Microsoft's built-in Linux layer, and the installer can set that up for you.

On a Mac, you need macOS on a reasonably recent machine, with 4 GB of RAM or more. One important detail: Macs come with two kinds of chip. Older Macs use Intel chips, and newer ones use Apple silicon, the M1, M2, M3 and later chips. Docker offers a different download for each, so check which chip you have under the Apple menu, in About This Mac, before downloading.

On Linux, you need a 64-bit distribution such as Ubuntu, Debian or Fedora, a user account that can use sudo, and an internet connection. The steps below use Ubuntu. If containers are still new to you, start with our explainer on what Docker is and how it works, then come back here with the idea clear in your head.

The Docker Docs Get Started overview (docs.docker.com) — the official starting point before you install Docker on any system.

How to Install Docker on Windows

Step 1: Go to the official Docker website and download Docker Desktop for Windows. Only download it from Docker itself, not from a random software site.

Step 2: Run the downloaded installer. When it asks about WSL 2, leave the option to use WSL 2 switched on. This is the setting beginners most often untick by accident, and Docker really wants it on.

Step 3: Follow the prompts, then restart your computer when the installer asks. The restart is not optional decoration; Windows needs it to finish setting up the Linux layer.

Step 4: Open Docker Desktop from the Start menu and wait until it says it is running. The first start can take a minute or two.

Step 5: Open PowerShell or Windows Terminal and run the verification commands shown later in this guide. If they work, your Windows install is done.

How to Install Docker on Mac

Step 1: Download Docker Desktop for Mac, choosing the version for your chip, Intel or Apple silicon, as explained above.

Step 2: Open the downloaded file and drag the Docker icon into your Applications folder, just like a normal Mac app.

Step 3: Launch Docker from Applications. macOS may ask for your password. Accept the prompts, because Docker needs permission to set up its background service.
